title: Refinance Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Refinance Calculator: Compare current and replacement loan payments, monthly savings and the months needed to recover refinancing costs. Learn how to use it,…
content:
The [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Compare current and replacement loan payments, monthly savings and the months needed to recover refinancing costs. Enter your current loan balance, current annual rate, remaining term, new annual rate, new term and refinancing costs paid upfront and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Refinancing replaces an existing loan with a new one, often to reduce the rate, change the term or alter the payment. A lower rate alone does not guarantee savings: upfront charges and resetting the clock on a long loan can outweigh the benefit. This calculator compares the current remaining schedule with a new fixed-rate loan and shows payment savings, cost recovery and lifetime interest under consistent principal-and-interest assumptions. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Refinance Calculator

Start by entering your current loan balance, then entering your current annual rate (%), entering your remaining term (years), entering your new annual rate (%), entering your new term (years) and finally entering your refinancing costs paid upfront. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the estimated payoff balance, current note rate and exact years remaining.
2. Enter the new rate and term, then add closing, arrangement, legal and other non-refundable refinancing costs.
3. Check cost recovery against how long you expect to keep the loan, then compare lifetime cost as well as monthly relief.

## Formula

Both payments use P·r ÷ (1−(1+r)⁻ⁿ). Cost recovery = upfront costs ÷ monthly payment reduction. Lifetime difference = old remaining interest − new interest − upfront costs.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Refinancing 280,000 from 7.25% to 6.25% over the same 25 years lowers the payment by roughly 184 per month. A 4,500 cost is recovered in about 25 months, before considering any penalties or tax effects. Try the same figures in the [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Current loan balance: 280000, Current annual rate: 7.25 %, Remaining term: 25 years, New annual rate: 6.25 %, New term: 25 years, Refinancing costs paid upfront: 4500), the [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) returns New monthly payment: 1,847.07, Monthly payment change: 176.78, Cost-recovery time: 26 months, Interest on current remaining schedule: 327,157.77, New interest plus upfront costs: 278,622.28, Lifetime cost difference: 48,535.49 saved. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Break-even is only one decision test

Cost-recovery months divide upfront costs by the monthly payment reduction. If you sell or refinance again before that point, the monthly saving may not repay the transaction costs. After break-even, payment savings can continue, but lifetime interest still depends on the new term. A fresh 30-year loan can cost more overall than keeping a loan with only 20 years left.

## Cash flow and total cost can pull in opposite directions

Extending a term may intentionally reduce a monthly commitment even when it increases lifetime interest. Shortening a term can do the reverse. The lifetime comparison here uses the current remaining term and the selected new term; it excludes tax effects, prepayment penalties, insurance changes and the return you might earn by investing monthly savings.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Ask whether costs are paid upfront or added to the balance; this calculator assumes upfront.
- Include any early-repayment charge on the current loan in refinancing costs.
- If payment reduction is your goal, still compare the extra years of interest before extending the term.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good refinance break-even period?

There is no universal cutoff. It should be comfortably shorter than the time you expect to keep the new loan, with allowance for uncertainty about moving or refinancing again. Try it with your own numbers in the [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does a lower rate always save money?

No. Fees and a longer repayment period can offset or exceed the interest-rate benefit, which is why lifetime cost is shown alongside the payment. You can use it as often as you like, and because nothing is uploaded, stored or tracked, there is nothing to delete afterwards.

### Are taxes and insurance included?

No. The comparison covers principal and interest only. Property tax, insurance and association dues normally continue independently of refinancing. Try it with your own numbers in the [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### When does refinancing make sense?

Usually when the new rate is meaningfully lower than your current rate and you will stay in the home long enough for the monthly savings to cover the closing costs. Compare the total cost, not just the monthly payment. Try it with your own numbers in the [Refinance Calculator](/refinance-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Refinance Calculator use?
